name: Gliclazide
route_note: oral tablet; modified-release once daily or immediate-release once/twice daily

discovery.note: A sulfonylurea with an azabicyclo-octyl ring developed by the French company Servier. Year of the patent; approved for medical use in 1972.

tagline: Servier's sulfonylurea, widely used outside the US and in the ADVANCE trial
summary: Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin secretion and is widely used for type 2 diabetes in Europe, Asia and Australia but is not approved in the United States. It has a lower risk of severe hypoglycaemia than glibenclamide and is the sulfonylurea listed by the WHO as an essential medicine.
mechanism: Gliclazide binds SUR1 on pancreatic beta cells, closing KATP channels, depolarising the membrane and triggering calcium-dependent insulin release. It is relatively selective for the beta-cell SUR1 over cardiac and vascular SUR2 isoforms.

It is metabolised to inactive products, which limits accumulation in kidney impairment compared with glibenclamide. Antioxidant and antiplatelet properties have been described in laboratory studies but their clinical relevance is uncertain.

history.title: Modified release
history.detail: Diamicron MR, a once-daily modified-release formulation, is introduced.

history.title: ADVANCE trial
history.detail: The ADVANCE trial uses gliclazide MR-based intensive control in 11,140 patients, reducing nephropathy (NEJM 2008).

history.title: UK first-line sulfonylurea
history.detail: Gliclazide is the most prescribed sulfonylurea in the UK and many Commonwealth countries, often as second-line after metformin.

history.title: TOSCA.IT
history.detail: TOSCA.IT, comparing pioglitazone with sulfonylureas (mostly gliclazide or glimepiride) added to metformin, finds no difference in cardiovascular events.

facts: Gliclazide has never been approved by the US FDA.
The ADVANCE trial's intensive arm targeted an HbA1c of 6.5% or below using gliclazide MR.

references.title: ADVANCE Collaborative Group. Intensive blood glucose control (NEJM 2008)
